staged_description.title: Trump Signed a 2025 Law Limiting Some IRA Wind and Solar Credits
staged_description.description_short: The 2025 reconciliation law ended certain IRA wind and solar electricity credits for covered facilities placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027.
staged_description.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, amended the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean-electricity production and investment credits. For covered wind and solar facilities, the law ends Sections 45Y and 48E credits for facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, subject to statutory rules. It did not repeal every IRA clean-energy credit.
staged_description.description_long: President Trump signed Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Sections 70512 and 70513 amend the Internal Revenue Code’s clean-electricity production credit under Section 45Y and clean-electricity investment credit under Section 48E. The statute provides that these credits do not apply to covered wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, and includes separate transition rules concerning when construction begins. The change narrows the period in which some Inflation Reduction Act clean-electricity credits can be claimed; it is more precise to describe it as a statutory termination for covered facilities than as blanket rescission of all IRA tax credits. Reuters’ July 2025 reporting described broader investment uncertainty after subsidy changes, but the statute is the stronger source for which credits and facilities are affected. The supplied row does not identify a credit-by-credit inventory, and this draft does not claim that all solar, wind, battery, electric-vehicle or already-committed projects lost support. The legal text establishes the cutoff and scope; project-specific eligibility depends on statutory definitions and transition provisions.

frozen_original.title: Mar-a-Lago Security: Foreign Nationals Freely Access President Across Both Terms
frozen_original.synopsis: Throughout both presidential terms, Trump's Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, operated as an open environment where paying members and their guests — including individuals from countries of counterintelligence concern — had routine access to spaces where the president and senior officials conducted meetings and discussions. Unlike the White House and official government facilities, Mar-a-Lago lacked SCIFs, had no classified communications infrastructure, and operated under commercial hospitality protocols rather than security-first principles. Intelligence officials in both terms described the club as a 'honeypot' for foreign intelligence services, with documented instances of Chinese, Russian, and other foreign nationals gaining proximity to the president and his advisors. The Secret Service's inability to screen all club contacts created persistent and unmitigated counterintelligence risks.
